tagline: Farm communities, inland lakes and a Cass River crossing beside the freeway corridor.
intro: M-15 connects Bay City and Clarkston through agricultural communities, crossing the Cass River at Vassar and passing inland lakes near Ortonville. The East Michigan Council of Governments presents this Pure Michigan Byway, also called the Pathway to Family Fun Recreational Heritage Route, as a diversion from I-75. It highlights village festivals, outdoor concerts, camping, fishing and hiking as the route’s recreational appeal. The council also points to Murphy Lake State Game Area a few miles from Millington, among the outdoor destinations along the corridor.

The present M-15 designation began after 1926 on a highway from Clarkston to Vassar. By the end of 1936 it extended into Bay City, sharing M-24’s route. Further extensions carried the number across Bay City to the freeway, but those were reversed in 1970. The northern end returned to Center Avenue, where it remains.

Traveling south from Center Avenue, follow Trumbull Street and Tuscola Road out of Bay City’s residential neighborhoods into farmland. Continue through Richville to Vassar’s Cass River crossing, then Millington, Otisville and Davison. At Otisville, State Road curves west of a group of small lakes before continuing through town. The southern stretch passes Goodrich and Ortonville, bending between Lake Louise and Bald Eagle Lake. In Clarkston it becomes Main Street near Parke Lake, before reaching US-24 south of town.

moments.title: Vassar
moments.text: The Cass River runs through Vassar, where M-15 crosses it on Huron Avenue. A dam was part of the founders’ plan: James M. Edmunds and Townsend North led four men seeking a place to build one and establish a city. They named Vassar for Edmunds’ uncle Matthew, later the founder of Vassar College. The county seat moved to Caro in 1860, while lumbering and related industries drove Vassar’s growth for the next thirty years. North’s ventures included a sawmill in 1849 and a woolen mill in 1867. After timber depletion and the 1881 Thumb Fire, the area shifted toward agriculture, with sugar beets important to its economy by 1900.

moments.title: Ortonville
moments.text: Ortonville grew at a milling center established by Amos Orton. He built a gristmill in 1852 and replaced it in 1856 with the structure at 366 Mill Street. Orton combined milling with work as a blacksmith and storekeeper, making the mill site a center for several of the settlement’s trades. The mill adopted roller processing in 1889 and generated electricity for the community during part of the 1920s. Milling continued until 1960. Emiline and Jack Hamilton donated the building to the Ortonville Community Historical Society in 1968. The hand-hewn timber-frame mill now serves as a local-history museum.
moments.notice: The mill is a timber-frame, two-and-a-half-story Greek Revival building.

moments.title: Clarkston
moments.text: Main Street carries M-15 through the Clarkston Village Historic District. The Clark brothers platted the village in 1842, ten years after Butler Holcomb built a house and sawmill here. Henry Ford later owned a mill powered by water from what is now Mill Pond. Part of that building survives, adapted as a small mall with art galleries and offices. The village received state historic recognition in 1976 and entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1979. Clarkston became an incorporated village in 1884 and a city in 1992, retaining “Village” within its official city name.
